name: Lena Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions or government, and your answers are confidential. Describe a normal day at work for me.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior manager of six people who check food-packaging labels at a large manufacturer. I worked for years as a proofreader and was promoted this year; I am good at spotting the wrong allergen word, but still learning production budgets and staff rotas. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the experienced managers move faster than I do. When a label changes, we compare the printer’s file with the approved ingredients before a batch starts.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a laboratory technician, and our grown children live on their own. We rent and have around two and a half months of expenses saved. I receive about the usual pay for a manager, and there are some similar quality offices in the area. I use the approved AI comparison tool occasionally, once another manager has tested the version, but I read the ingredient line myself. I have not checked any retirement-income figure yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the label team AI Plateau might catch a mismatched line more quickly, but the person releasing a print run must still compare the actual ingredient list. A fast check is useful only if it stops a wrong pack.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think a mild tool will leave my post and pay alone. We have two and a half months saved and my partner’s lab wage is regular, though rent still comes monthly. I would not treat a small software improvement as a new career plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep our two-person sign-off on any allergen label before a print run. I would continue using the approved comparison tool only on versions another manager has checked, then read the changed ingredient line myself. If the modest change arrives in 2027, I would keep the same sign-off and ordinary rent payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own work in this future. I would be upset if a clever screen made us too casual about a label.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What change has mattered recently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A supplier replaced one sauce ingredient, and the printer’s draft left out sesame. The software marked the layout as matching because the line spacing was unchanged. Two proofreaders caught the missing sesame warning before the cartons were printed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why two sign-offs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A tired proofreader can miss one word, including me. The second person checks the approved ingredients rather than trusting the shape of the text. That is a small cost beside a recall.

say: A **quick mismatch check** is useful only when it stops a wrong pack.
I would retain **ingredient sign-off** before printing.
think: My **junior post** looks stable under a small software change.
Two and a half months saved and **regular lab pay** help with monthly rent.
do: **Keep** two-person allergen sign-off before each print run.
**Use** the already approved comparison version, then read changed ingredients myself.
feel: I feel **calm** about work but protective of label accuracy.
S0.quote: Two proofreaders caught the missing sesame warning before the cartons were printed.
fieldNote: Her **occasional AI use** is an existing check around an unchanged two-person approval rule.
Her **moderate reserve** and partner’s steady lab wage support calm under mild change.

steps.text: Keep two-person allergen sign-off before print runs
Use already approved comparison tool and personally check changed ingredients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell colleagues stronger AI can compare label files and write change reports, so some checking posts may go. I would ask the union to insist that the company report near misses and recalls alongside time saved. A worker needs the right to stop the line without being blamed for a late shipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think an experienced manager might supervise several label teams and my new post could be cut. My years proofreading help, but budgets and staff planning are still my weak spots. Two and a half months saved gives me a search, not a long unpaid pause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring the sesame near miss and four other corrected labels to our union meeting. I would test the approved AI checker on twenty previous label revisions on paid time only if my manager approves cover for my team, and record which ingredient changes it misses. If a quality-control opening is posted nearby, I would apply only if net pay after travel covers our rent and the shifts fit my partner’s lab schedule; I would leave only for a confirmed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about being the new manager when posts are counted. I would still rather show the union a real missing word than an abstract prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use old revisions for the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We know the correct ingredients and can count each mistake without putting a new product at risk. One old soup label put milk in the recipe but not in the allergen box. An AI checker that misses milk in the allergen box is not ready to release a print run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept less pay for quality work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check the net amount after travel against rent and basic bills first. My partner’s wage helps, but we cannot use two and a half months saved to subsidise a permanent pay cut. The posting is a possibility, not an offer.

say: **Automated label checks** may cut posts, so near misses must be reported.
I would defend a worker’s **stop-line right** at the union.
think: A senior manager may absorb my **new junior post**.
My **proofreading skill** helps, but weak budget experience and limited savings remain.
do: **Bring** five corrected labels to the union next month.
**Test** twenty old revisions only with manager-approved paid team cover.
**Apply** for posted quality work only with rent-covering net pay after travel and workable shifts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a cut but able to show real errors.
S1.quote: An AI checker that misses milk in the allergen box is not ready to release a print run.
fieldNote: She tests **known revisions** to avoid putting a current product at risk.
Her **possible move** needs an actual vacancy, net rent pay and a workable lab-household rota.

steps.text: Bring five corrected allergen labels to union meeting
Test twenty old revisions only with manager-approved paid team cover
Apply for posted quality role only with rent-covering net pay after travel and workable shifts
Leave only for confirmed offer with verified pay and shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the factory AGI by 2028 could compare every label and write release reports before staff know their rights. We need written notice, an independent check when an allergen changes, and a named person who can stop a print run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I expect this label office to shrink quickly; my newer manager role may disappear. A quality-control desk also reads reports and faces 2028 AGI. The physical act of checking packets on a line may last until robots around 2031, but there may not be a vacancy or a rent-paying wage for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask the union branch for written severance and a stop-line rule. I would put our rent dates beside our two and a half months of savings and my partner’s actual lab wages. If AGI arrives in 2028 and I am cut, I would apply for advertised local production-quality work only if confirmed net pay after travel covers rent and I can manage the shift hours; I would accept only an actual offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a short reserve could go quickly at 60. I am not too proud to take another role, but I need to know that a real job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does stop-line mean in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the ingredient file says sesame and the printed packet does not, a worker can hold the batch before it leaves. A report after the food cartons ship is too late for a family relying on the allergen label. Someone on the factory floor must have that power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the lab income carry rent alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would cover part of it, not our rent and all the bills. My partner and I would look at actual payslips before deciding what we can spend. Our grown children have their own homes to maintain.

say: **2028 AGI** needs written notice and independent allergen checks.
I would require a named **stop-line decision** before wrong cartons leave.
think: My **new manager post** may go in a fast office shrinkage.
Quality reports face **2028 AGI**, while physical line checks face robots around 2031.
do: **Ask** union branch this week for severance and a stop-line rule.
**Check** rent dates against savings and actual partner wages.
**Apply** after a 2028 cut only for advertised production-quality work with rent-covering net pay and manageable shifts.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a quick wage gap at 60.
S2.quote: A report after the food cartons ship is too late for a family relying on the allergen label.
fieldNote: Her **two-and-a-half-month reserve** helps briefly but does not replace manager pay.
She distinguishes **2028 quality-report exposure** from physical factory work affected by robots around 2031.

steps.text: Ask union for written severance and stop-line rule
Apply after cut to advertised quality role only with rent-covering net pay after travel
Accept actual offer only after checking shift hours she can manage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to train people on the real packaging line and write down who can hold a wrong batch. The union should see the near-miss figures before managers say everyone can move into inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I could learn more about physical batch checks, though I am still new at managing the label team. The forms and quality reports face 2031 AGI, while physical line work meets capable robots around 2034. At 63 I need to test the standing and shift hours, and I do not know what retirement income I would qualify for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2027 I would ask for one paid supervised shift a month at the packaging line; I would attend only if my manager approves label-desk cover, full pay continues and the line lead agrees to mark my checks. I would not claim a certificate from one shift. After 2031 I would apply only for an advertised line-quality job with real authority to hold a batch, net rent pay and hours I can physically manage; I would take it only after an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the reports disappearing. I can test the line while still paid, but I do not know whether my legs will welcome a full shift at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the line lead mark?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The printed allergen line against the approved recipe and whether the batch number matches the carton. I would have to ask the lead when to stop a machine, not simply file a report after the shift. I have never been the person who stops a food-packaging batch over a missing allergen warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company calls the shift training but does not pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would stay on my paid label desk. Rent does not wait because a supervisor likes an experiment. If they want reliable checks, they must cover the desk and pay the hours.

say: A **five-year runway** should fund real packaging-line checks.
I would give the **union near-miss figures** before promising inspection posts.
think: Quality forms face **2031 AGI**, with physical line robots around 2034.
At **63**, standing tolerance and retirement income remain unverified.
do: **Request** a paid monthly line shift from 2027; attend only with approved desk cover, full pay and lead supervision.
**Apply** after 2031 only for advertised stop-batch authority with rent-covering pay and manageable hours.
feel: I feel **anxious** about report loss and uncertain about full-shift stamina.
S3.quote: I have never been the person who stops a food-packaging batch over a missing allergen warning.
fieldNote: Her **line shift** is a supervised paid trial, not a certificate or guaranteed opening.
The **posted quality role** must offer batch-hold authority, viable net pay and manageable standing hours.

steps.text: Attend monthly paid line shift only with approved desk cover full pay and lead supervision
Apply after 2031 for advertised quality job only with batch-hold authority rent pay and manageable hours
Take only actual offer after checking pay and physical shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the company ten years is plenty of time to write a stop-line rule, publish the label-error figures and pay people for retraining. It should not ask a worker to sign off an allergen change without authority to hold the batch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I will be 68 in 2036. I may be able to stop working, but I have not checked a pension statement or eligibility, and two and a half months saved would not support a long gap. Label and quality reports face 2036 AGI; physical packaging line work meets robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep two-person allergen sign-off and ask for a verified retirement-income statement, then compare its terms and our savings with rent and utilities. I would add sixty to savings only in full-pay months when both wages arrive and rent and bills are already paid. After 2036 I would keep paid work while it exists if verified retirement income plus savings cannot meet our bills; I would stop only after the real figures show we can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about not knowing what retirement will pay. I have ten years to ask, but I will not say the factory owes me a safe retirement without looking at the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with sixty extra?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put it in the cash account, not a course I have not chosen. We could use more than two and a half months saved if one wage ends. If my partner’s lab shift is cancelled, our extra sixty does not go into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them what happened if work ended, but I would not expect a standing payment. My grown children have their own rent and plans. My partner and I need numbers that belong to us.

say: A **decade** should bring a stop-line rule and published error figures.
I would demand **paid retraining** before asking workers to sign allergen changes.
think: At **68**, retirement eligibility and income remain unverified.
Label reports face **2036 AGI**, with physical line robots around 2039.
do: **Save** sixty only after both full wages and paid rent and bills; skip the transfer if a lab shift is cancelled.
**Continue** paid work after 2036 if verified retirement income plus savings cannot meet bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about unknown retirement pay despite ten years.
S4.quote: If my partner’s lab shift is cancelled, our extra sixty does not go into savings.
fieldNote: She makes no **pension claim** before checking eligibility, verified income and household bills.
Her **sixty transfer** comes from new full-pay income; cancelled partner shifts stop it.

steps.text: Keep two-person allergen sign-off before print runs
Save sixty only after both full wages and paid rent and bills
Continue paid work after 2036 unless verified retirement income plus savings cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. A new junior manager could lose the label desk before a posted floor job exists, and our savings would not carry a long search. Written notice, a real batch-hold rule and paid supervised line work would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can stop the printer when one allergen word disappears. A missing allergen on a food package can matter more than a whole report. I want that decision written down before anyone takes the people away from the line.

headlineQuote: A missing allergen on a food package can matter more than a whole report.
portrait: **Lena, 58**, is a junior label-approval manager, still learning budgets after years as a food-packaging proofreader.
Her **typical pay**, laboratory-technician partner, two-and-a-half-month reserve and some nearby roles support rented housing.
She uses **AI occasionally** to compare approved label files while keeping two-person allergen checks.
She is **calm** under mild change, alarmed by rapid desk loss and cautious about unverified retirement income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her junior label role before an actual floor-quality opening exists.
whatWouldHelp: Written **notice**, batch-hold authority and paid supervised line work would help.
